blocks.text: IN your Life of the Right Reverend Bishop Bull, the principal, and indeed the Only Considerable Objection you allege against my Book, is; that almost all my Citations out of that Learned Author are represented in a very different View from That which the Author had certainly in writing those Passages; as are also the Citations out of the Fathers themselves, which Dr. Clarke here met with, and both accommodated to his own purpose, and That frequently without so much as the least Notice taken of the Explications and Answers given to them by Bishop Bull. But still, notwithstanding this reasonable Acknowledgment, you continue to allege, that it is enough to have shewn what manner of Judgement we ought to make of Dr Clarke's Citations, for they are generally applied much after the same Manner and with the same Views; and you call it (in a less kind manner than usual,) the Doctors Artful Way of citing Authors and Books, and infinate that therefore my Quotations are not much to be depended upon. That sometimes they are not indeed much to be depended upon, for knowing (as you say) the Opinion or Judgment of any Writer; is very true, because they were not brought for That Purpose: But then they are very much to be depended upon for another and far more material reason, viz. for knowing the Truth itself of Things. And in order to This End, they are always so much the more to be depended upon, and the more to be regarded; as the Author, from whom they are cited, was upon the whole more different in his Opinion, from what those particular Citations seem to express. For Writers upon controversial Points, feldom make more Concessions in favour of any opinion different from their own, than the Weight of Truth and

Wherefore in citing and making Use of such Concessions, there is no other Artfulness, than that most justifiable one of drawing Arguments strong and conclusive from such Premises, as even an Adversary is of necessity forced to grant. Nor needs it at all to be regarded, that some of the Writers, from whom such Citations are taken, do themselves indeavour sometimes to draw Conclusions very different. For in all Argumentation whatsoever, it is well known that the Premises only are of any Weight; and that Conclusions always stand for nothing, except the Reader finds himself compelled to draw them, as well as the Writer. Nevertheless, though the Truth of the Scripture-Doctrine does not at all depend upon it, yet, for the satisfaction of such as are apt to pay a greater deference to Authority than is reasonable, I shall not omit taking this occasion to assure you, that, as far as I am able to judge from the whole Course and Tenour of the Writings of the Antients, All the passages cited in my whole Book from the following Principal Writers, viz. Clemens Romanus, Ignatius, Justin, Irenaeus, Origen, Novatian and Eusebius, are not only particular Concessions, but do express what seems moreover to have been in the whole the real Sentiments of the respective Writers themselves: And in the First Part

This is very plainly the Doctrine of Scripture, whatever had been the Opinion of the Catholick Fathers. But neither, in Truth, is This Assertion at all contrary (as you conceive it to be) to the Mind of the Catholick Fathers; much less, from the Defense of the Nicene Faith doth it appear (as you suppose,) to be contrary to the Mind of those Fathers. blocks.text: ble, &c. I have abridged your words, but I am perfwaded your Candour will not complain that I have in the least altered your Sense. Now in every part of this Reasoning of yours, there is (I think) something defective. For how many Other Attributes and Perfections soever, Origen in his Book ascribes to the Son; yet unless he ascribed Supremacy also, (which he no where does, but on the contrary every where expressly and with great caution excludes it,) this cannot at all affect the Question: See my Scripture-doctrine, pag. 359 and 266. And though he had indeed in Other clear and undoubted passages (which yet he no where has) asserted the Son to be Supreme as well as the Father; yet it would not at all follow (unless Origen were a Writer infallibly consistent with himself,) that he did not interpret the particular text referred to, in the manner that I affirmed him to interpret it. And though Bp. Bull does indeed indeavour to show, that Origen in the place here referred to, speaks of Christ as an Exemplar in his humane Nature; yet he expressly acknowledges [si daremus Origenem ibi loqui de Christo quatenus Deus est,—baud minus recte ea ratione Patri primas tribuere potuit,] that if it be granted that Origen there speaks concerning Christ as God, yet—as deriving—from the Fountain of the Father, he might rightly.

Now in every part of this Reasoning of yours, there is (I think) something defective. For how many Other Attributes and Perfections soever, Origen in his Book ascribes to the Son; yet unless he ascribed Supremacy also, (which he no where does, but on the contrary every where expressly and with great caution excludes it,) this cannot at all affect the Question: See my Scripture-doctrine, pag. 359 and 266. And though he had indeed in Other clear and undoubted passages (which yet he no where has) asserted the Son to be Supreme as well as the Father; yet it would not at all follow (unless Origen were a Writer infallibly consistent with himself,) that he did not interpret the particular text referred to, in the manner that I affirmed him to interpret it. And though Bp. Bull does indeed indeavour to show, that Origen in the place here referred to, speaks of Christ as an Exemplar in his humane Nature; yet he expressly acknowledges [si daremus Origenem ibi loqui de Christo quatenus Deus est,—baud minus recte ea ratione Patri primas tribuere potuit,] that if it be granted that Origen there speaks concerning Christ as God, yet—as deriving—from the Fountain of the Father, he might rightly.

As to the distinction you allege, that here is not the least Word said, that can justly be interpreted of the Son's Inferiority to the Father in NATURE, but rather the contrary: I shall not contend with you about metaphysical Words, which since I have constantly avoided because of their Abstract and Ambiguous Signification, you should not have chosen to use them in representing my Sense. Bishop Bull expressly owns the Person of the Son to be, in his Highest Capacity, subordinate to the Person of the Father: Which is a Notion very intelligible, (whatever be the Nature, Substance or Essence of either;) and is all (I think) that the Honour of God and the Whole Doctrine of Scripture obliges us to contend for. The Word, Nature, (as it signifies the Nature of any Person, abstract from the Person himself,) is a Metaphysical Term, of great Ambiguity and Obscureness, and of no Use that I know of in any Question, but to introduce more Difficulties by dark Expressions, than are really found in the Things themselves.

blocks.text: ing of it being, that——Christ appearing to the Holy Men under the Old Testament, received from them divine Honours, and was manifested to them by the most High Name of God. Mr Bull first proveth &c. — And there is nothing in this whole Method, nor in any particular Argument under it, which doth tend in the least to favour such an Inequality of NATURE in Father and Son, as is included in That Scheme which it is brought to support. The passage here referred to, are those words of the learned Bp. Bull, wherein he declares and approves the opinion of the Antient Fathers, that the Angel of the Lord (Acts 7, 30,) which appeared to Moses in the Bush, and said, I am the God of thy Fathers, was the Son appearing in his Fathers Name. Now since the Scripture every where represents the Father, as absolutely Invisible; and those Antient Writers, whose Opinions Bp Bull cites and approves, always suppose it impious to imagine that the Supreme God and Father of All ever appeared visibly in his own Person; the Inference I designed should be drawn from hence, is, that the Person of the Son is Subordinate to the Person of the Father, whose Angel or Messenger he is, and in whose Name and by whose Mission he appears. All this, the learned Bp. makes no scruple to grant; and therefore 'twas no misrepresentation of his words, to cite them

This Fourth passage, you say, seemeth indeed to be very much to the Purpose; and every one that reads it as it is cited, and will not be at the pains to consult either what follows it, or what is there distinctly referred to, may be easily led to think, that our Author [Bp. Bull] was not a Defender, but an Underminer of the Nicene Faith, by maintaining the Son, even AS HE IS GOD, to be LESS than the Father: Which though it be most true in a certain sense which He hath explained, in conformity to Primitive Testimonies, and to the Confession of the Council of Nice itself, as He is God of God; yet is both diametrically opposite to his plain Meaning, and to what he defended for the Catholick Faith with so much strength, if thereby it be understood that there is Greater and Less in the divine Nature and Essence. A Notion expressed with such Solemnity as This, is what an ignorant and unprejudiced person, hearing it thus delivered, would immediately expect to find in every page of his Bible, and of all Antient Christian Authors, and in every part of the Forms now used in the Church: Whereas, in Truth, both the word [Essence] itself, and the Phrase [in the Unity of the Divine Essence,] are merely Scholastick and Metaphysical Terms, of very uncertain Signification, (as any one will find, when he indeavours to declare what he means by them;) not Once found in the whole New Testament, nor in the Orthodox Fathers of the First Ages, nor in any part of the Articles or Liturgy of the Church of England, which are its most publick and authentic Acts. Now of What Use can the introducing such new Terms be? For either they have no determinate Signification at all: Or else they are intended to express the same Doctrine, which is taught in Scripture; And then, why could not That Doctrine have been as well and better expresst by you in those same words, which the Wisdom of God thought most proper to express it in? Or else, lastly, they express something different from what is taught in Scripture; and then

blocks.text: The Excuse, which you (who know well how to write with the greatest Temper yourself) are willing to make for Others who write without That Spirit of Meekness and Christianity, is a very charitable one; viz. that they think they obey the Apostolical Injunction of Contending Earnestly for the Faith. But This, though it will indeed excuse much Zeal, yet it will not excuse Wrath and Uncharitableness. For, the Wrath of Man worketh not the Righteousness of God. And, as far as I have been able to observe, those persons have always been in proportion most hot and angry, whose Doctrine has been least agreeable to Scripture, and who have been much less concerned for the Doctrine delivered TO, than for That which (as you well observe, pag. 24,) was delivered BY the Saints, that is, by those Writers whose opinions they happened most to like.

I am sure I have represented this Objection of yours, in its full force. The Reader will observe, that 'tis an Objection ad hominem only, and nothing at all to the Merits of any question concerning the Truth or Erroneousness of any Opinion or Doctrine. Nevertheless, because 'tis indeed a very Important Objection ad hominem, I will indeavour to explain myself very distinctly to you upon it. With respect to Civil matters,

blocks.text: Faith, but as prudential Means of Uniformity, and of preventing Disorder and Confusion among themselves. And when in such Forms there be (as there generally are) Expressions which at first sight look different ways, (as I have shown there are more Expressions in the Liturgy of the Church of England expressly for me in the present Controversy, than there are which seem to be against me;) it cannot be, but Men must be allowed to interpret what is obscure, by that which seems to them more plain and scriptural. Every Man that (for the sake of Peace and Order) affents to, or makes use of, any such Forms of Humane Appointment; is obliged to reconcile them with what appears to Him to be the Doctrine of Scripture, and take care to understand them in such a Sense only, as is consistent with That Doctrine: Otherwise he parts with his Christianity, for the sake of a Civil and political Religion. It becomes a sincere Man, (especially if he varies from Notions commonly received,) to Declare plainly in what Sense he understands any words of humane Institution; that his Inferiors and Equals may not be imposed upon by him, and that his Superiours may judge of such Declaration. That the Sense in which any Human Forms appear to a Mans self to be consistent with Scripture, and not the presumed Meaning of the Compilers,

And That Article in the Nicene Creed, [of One Substance with the Father,] is now (through the Ambiguity of the Latin and English Translation,) by most Men taken much otherwise, than the Council intended it: For the greater part of Modern Christians, (if we may judge by the Writings of eminent Divines,) understand it (as if it had been παυτοῦς) to signify, of one INDIVIDUAL Substance with the Father; Whereas all learned Men know, that the Greek word *[ομοθέσας] never had any such Signification, and that the Council meant no such thing; but, of the same KIND of Substance with the Father: [Εὐκ ἐν διαίας τῶν πάλεος, so the Council of Nice explained themselves, though those words are now left out of the Creed;] The Son was, they said, γεννητείς οἱ παλείως, τῶν περὶ τῶν πάλεος. begotten of the Father, that is, from the Substance of the Father: And therefore was not (which Notion was then universally condemned) himself That individual Substance from which he was begotten. But their meaning was; he was produced, not from any Other Substance, (as Man was formed from the Dust of the Earth,) but, after an ineffable manner, from the Substance of the Father only. Which Sense of theirs, is Now generally mistaken. I see no possible Remedy for These

blocks.text: that Men of All Seets and Opinions whatsoever, are apt to plead Scripture in their own Defense. The true Meaning of which observation is, that Men of almost Any Opinion may pick out some single Texts, which, when taken by themselves, shall seem to look in Favour of That Opinion. But the Method I used, was to set forth in One View ALL the Texts that in any manner related to the matter in Question; and, by comparing them together, I showed how they might All be reconciled in one uniform and consistent Scheme. Your learned Friend has not taken That Method; And therefore, had there been more Texts alleged, and more favourable to him, than Any of them really are; yet This would not have Proved any thing.

blocks.label: text
blocks.text: when he says, OF him as HE is Father, THROUGH him as HE is Son, TO him as HE is the Holy Ghost. All which Notions are inconsistent with, and contradictory to, each other. For if they be All one and the same individual Being, how can one and the same individual Being be subordinate to itself? And if HE who is Father, be also himself both Son and Holy Ghost; then it will follow, that there is no divine Nature of Christ at all, but that Christ was only a great Prophet, in whom God the Father manifested himself extraordinarily; Which is downright Socinianism. So that indeed it is impossible your Friend's Arguments should be conclusive to prove any thing, when he does not so much as know distinctly what 'tis he intends to prove. Neither can he allege, that these things are a Mystery: For the most evident Contradictions are not a whit more mysterious, than the most evident Truths.

N° 1.
MATT. XIX, 17. There is none Good, but One, that is, God.
Upon This Text I observed, that the word, One, according to the Nature of the Greek and Latin Languages, [εις, Unus,] must of necessity signify, One Person.
This, your learned Friend denies; and contends that it may as well or better signify, One Being. His Reafons are,
That the word, One, $ [\varepsilon_{\mathrm{os}}] $ is Masculine, by reason of its relation to God, $ [\Theta \varepsilon_{\mathrm{os}}] $
That it is no less fitted to represent Being, than Person; since they are neither of them Masculine.
That the fame word, $ [\tilde{\epsilon}_{i s}, ] $ is used for One Thing, Gal. 3, 28, Ye are all One, $ [\tilde{\epsilon}_{i s}]$ in Christ Jesus. Not One Person, for That (he says) is impossible; but, One Thing.
That the Vulgar Latin renders it fo, [Unum estis,] Ye are One thing or body.
That Theodoret and Theophylae, (and doubtless the Greeks were proper Judges of their own Language,) explain it as signifying, $ \tilde{\nu} $ σῶμα, One Body.
Laftly,
In the Scripture-doctrine, N° 1 & 340. In the Answer, pag. I.

'Tis certain that Arguments run very low indeed, when all Grammar is forced to be reversed in such a manner, as would make every Language a mere Babel of words, without Any determinate Signification. blocks.text: But the word [ἐς] One, may in this Text (he says) be Masculine, by reason of its relation to God, [ὁεῖς.] I answer; This cannot possibly be, because Then (the same being to be said of ἐς also,) the full construction would be, There is None Good, [὇δεις αγαθός, there is no God Good,] but One God, that is God: Whereas the plain construction is, There is no Person Good, but One Person, which is God. Had our Saviour meant to say, (as he might, very properly,) There is no Being Good, but One, that is, God; (which yet would not have denoted That sort of Goodness which is Moral, but that which is Natural or Metaphysical;) he must have expressed it thus, ἐδεν αγαθόν, εἰ μη εν, οὐ θεὸς: in like manner as the Philosopher says, ἐδεν γολαςιπυς, εἰ μη εν, οὐ ανρρωπος, [Nibil risibile est, nift Unum, nempe Homo;] Nothing is capable of Laughter, but only One thing, namely Man, or, the Species of Mankind. Had he said, ἐδειες γολαςιπυς εἰ μη εν, οὐ ανρρωπιο, [Nemo risibilis, nift Unus, nempe Homo;] No One [that is, No Person] is capable of Laughter, but One, namely Man, or Mankind; the Expression had been manifestly absurd:

But This is a great mistake: For the word, Person, is always express both in Greek and Latin by the Masculine Adjective, and by It Only; there being no other word either in Greek or Latin, by which it ever was or can possibly be express. Persona, and დენისთი, and მორჩალი, are all of them words of a quite different Sense, and never used by any good Author (unless in very figurative Constructions) in this Signification. The Schoolmen have indeed, in their barbarous Language, made Hypostasis to signify Person; but what they mean by the word, they themselves know not.

Thus likewise in the passage before us, Gal. 3, 27, Ye have put on Christ; There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither Bond nor Free, there is neither Male nor Female; for ye are all [ἐς,] considered as One Person in Christ Jesus. Your learned Friend did not at all perceive the Elegancy and Beauty of the Apostle's Expression in this Place. Consider the Church as One Thing, as a Congregation or Body of Men, and all these natural Relations still continue distinct; But consider it under the Notion of one Person, the Spouse of Christ, and then all these differences and distinctions vanish. By the same Figure of Speech, the Jewish Church is stiled in Scripture the Daughter of Sion: Nations and Empires are, in the Prophecy of Daniel, personated as Kings: The Church in the Revelation, under Persecution, is a Woman flying into the Wilderness: The False Church abusing the temporal Power of Princes, to persecute good Christians; is the Woman, the Whore, riding upon a Scarlet-coloured (or bloody) Beast. World, who confess not that Jesus Christ is come in the Flesh; This is [ο πλανῶς οὐ αντίχειδος] The Deceiver and The Anti-Christ. You see, Sir, your learned Friend concluded somewhat too fast, when he thought he had put an end to the Criticism of Personality founded upon the Term, εἰς, Unus.
Well; but the Vulgar Latin (he says) renders it, [Unum estis,] Ye are One Thing or Body. I acknowledge it: And 'tis a great confirmation of what I have said. For, the Reason why the Author of That Translation did not render it Unus, as Beza rightly does; was because he knew that Unus could not possibly signify any thing else than One Person: Which He not apprehending how it could stand in that place, nor perceiving the Beauty of St Paul's similitude; instead therefore of rendring the Apostles word which he understood not, he put in another of his own which he understood better, and thereby altered and quite spoiled the Apostles Sense.
Theodoret and Theophylae, were not Translators, but Commentators. They therefore might justly paraphrase the Apostles Expression, by the Phrase [ἐν σώμα] One Body. I answer: When God the Father is thus stiled The One God; Idols, in opposition to him, are excluded hereby from being Gods at all; and the Son, in subordination to him, is excluded, not from being truly God, but from being That Person, That Supreme, Independent, Self-existent Governour of All, who, upon these accounts, is stiled, by way of Eminence, the One and Only God, while the Son is nevertheless, by communication of divine Power and Dominion from the Father, really and truly God. I think, in This only; that, after allowing a clear distinction, he still contends for such an unintelligible way of speaking, as either necessarily introduces, or at least cannot be vindicated from introducing, a Confusion of Persons.
As to his Citations from the Fathers upon this Head; though I do not think myself at all concerned to reconcile to each other the different ways of speaking found in the Fathers; yet I cannot but desire the Reader to compare the Few Places here cited by your Friend out of Three Fathers, with ten times the Number of places cited by Me out of the Same and many More Fathers, in my Scripture-doctrine, Part II, § 9. By which it will appear, that Much the greater Number of Ancient Writers declare themselves with the greatest possible distinctness to have understood This and the like Texts, exactly as I do; and that Those who speak more confusedly, (as when Tertullian says, Deus se Unicum, fed cum Filio, oftendit; God declares himself to be One only, but yet together with his Son;) did not mean, as your learned Friend does, [Deum & Filium esse unicum,] that God and the Son of God were One Individual; but, that God was so One, [ut tamen Filium ba-beret,]

JO H. XVII, 3. That they might know Thee, the Only True God; and Jesus Christ, whom thou hast sent.
These words, it hath been supposed, may be understood Two ways.
Either Thus : That they might know Thee, the Only True God ; and [that they might know] Jesus Christ, whom thou hast sent.
Or Thus: That they might know Thee, the Only True God; and Jesus Christ whom thou hast sent,[the Only True God also.]
The former is, I think, the True Sense of the words; your learned Friend thinks the latter to be so.

If the Term God, says he, can be applied to the Holy Ghost, [for Proof whereof he refers to five Texts, in not one of which the Term is so applied;] why should there be so much pains taken to prove it to belong to the Father, who is not mentioned in the Context? blocks.text: lutely as in this Text, signified, not the Father, but either the Holy Spirit or the whole Three Persons; it would follow that the Holy Spirit of God, was the Holy Spirit of Himself; which is a manifest Absurdity. The only Argument your Friend urges, why the word, God, in this Text, should be meant of the Holy Ghost, and not of the Father; is This very obscure one: That if the word God here signified the Father, then it would follow that the Holy Ghost acted by the Authority of the Father; which since the Apostles themselves also did, it would follow that They might have been stiled the Objects of the Lie, as well as the Holy Ghost; the Person of the Spirit being as little affected with the Lie spoken, in comparison of the Authority affronted in Him, as the Persons of the Apostles were affected by it in comparison of the Authority affronted in Them; Neither could a Lie against the Holy Ghost, have been said comparatively to be none against Men, if the Holy Ghost were not He who is here stiled God. I am sure I have represented his Argument more clear and strong, than the Author himself represented it; and yet at the best it is a very obscure one. The Strength of it indeed, is no more than this: If the Holy Ghost be at all subordinate to the Father, (as the Scripture every where declares he is sent and given by Him.)

G A L. IV, 8. Te did Service unto them which by Nature are no Gods, [τοῦς μὲν φύσει δοσια θεοῖς, or, as it is in the Alexandrian MS, τοῦς φύσει μὲν δοσια θεοῖς.]
Of these words I proposed the Two following Expositions.
1. Unto Gods, which have no Being in Nature, or which in Nature [in reality] have no Being.
2. Unto Beings, which by their Nature are not capable of having any divine Power or Authority: Thus, Acts 19, 26, they be no Gods; that is, they have none of that Authority and Dominion over you, which you ascribe to them.
Of the latter of these Expositions, your Learned Friend takes not the least Notice. I suppose, he overlooked it, as not being in its proper place, but in the Addenda, pag. 1; Though he elsewhere takes Notice of something else mentioned in That Page.

Against the former of them, He argues as follows :
1. That the Two most Antient Versions, the Vulgar and the Syriac, agree with our received Translation of the words.
2. That in St Paul's style of Writing, $ \varphi v \sigma s $ is no where used for Nature in general, or the System of Natural Beings.
3. That, had φύσας been used by him in that general Notion, yet, according to the Analogy of his Style in other places, he would rather have said ἐν φύσας, than φύσαι alone, if he had meant in Nature and not by Nature.
4. That if φύσθ had signified in Nature, yet 'tis probable the Apostle would rather have said τοῖς μὲν ἐσπαι alone, than τοῖς φύσει μὲν ἐσπαι.
5. That $ \varphi \iota \upsilon \sigma \epsilon $ is often used by the same Apostle in other places, to signify by Nature, not in Nature.
All these Criticisms of your Learned Friend, (which I have here fairly set before my Reader,) I acknowledge to be Right; And they are, by much, the most Scholarlike Observations in his Whole Book.

All Worship or Honour is Personal, paid not to a Metaphysical Substance, but to an Intelligent Agent ;) it follows manifestly, that so far as Dominion and Power and Authority is ascribed to any Being, more than it really has; so far That Being is merely [εἰδω]ov,] an Idol, a Nothing in the World, i Cor. 8, 4, a mere Fiction of the Imagination. When therefore St Paul here char-
ges the * Heathens, (or perhaps, as the Context seems to suppose, corrupt Jews and Worshippers of Angels,) with doing Service to Them which by Nature are no Gods; 'tis evident his Argument is not, that the Gods they worshipped were not absolutely Supreme. Self-existent, Independent Beings ;
(for They did not pretend This, nor does the Word ever signifie any such thing;) but that, neglecting the Worship of the True God, they worshipped Gods who had really nothing of That Nature which was ascribed to them; none of that Authority or Dominion, either Supreme or Subordinate, which These Men (like the Church of Rome Now in the case of their Saint-Worship,) imagined them to have. For they were Gods, which either had no Being at all; Fictions, and mere imaginary Deities: Or

blocks.text: Or else, at best, they were [διαμύνα] Beings which in reality were not of That Nature which their Worshippers pretended them to be, induced or capable of being induced with divine invisible Dominion and Authority over Men. blocks.text: I do acknowledge (and I observed it before in my Scripture-doctrine,) that the words [ἐνεσιοι οὖπιν τῶν θεῶν μμώτων, χὴ σωτήρ Ιποσὺς χειτῶν,] may, in true grammatical Construction, equally be rendred, either, The Righteousness of our God, and of our Saviour Jesus Christ, or, The Righteousness of our God and Saviour Jesus Christ. So that, if one Man thinks the word, God, is here meant of the Father, and another thinks that it is rather applied in this place to the Son; Neither of their Opinions can be demonstrably disproved.

blocks.label: text

blocks.label: text
blocks.text: My Reasons for understanding it of the Father, are: First, because the word, God, throughout the New Testament, generally signifies the Father, and therefore most probably does so in this place likewise. And Secondly, because in the very next Verse, the same words are repeated in such a Construction, as determines the Sense necessarily without Any Ambiguity; [ἐπὶν γνωστὸς τῆς θεωρὸς, ὑπ'ησθὸς τῆς κυείαν ἡμψώ] The Knowledge of God, and of Jesus our Lord. Now since, in the second Verse, these words, [The Knowledge of God, and of Jesus our Lord,] are in the Original placed in such a Construction, as of necessity to signify God the Father in Contradistinction to Jesus our Lord; 'tis probable that, in the first Verse likewise, those words, [The Righteousness of God, and our Saviour Jesus Christ,] though placed ambiguously in the Original, yet were intended in the same manner to signify God the Father, in Contradistinction to Jesus our Saviour.

blocks.text: As to the Text itself, the True Meaning of it seems to Me to be this: That in the like Sense as God the Father is in other places of Scripture declared to be the One and Only God, he is in this place declared to be also the One and Only Good. That is to say: As God the Father is, by way of Eminence, the One and Only God, because He Alone has [ἀντοθεόπτα] Divinity absolutely of Himself, Supreme, Unoriginate, and not derived from Any; (as Origen learnedly and at large argues in the place before-cited; See above, pag. 65.) and yet Christ is also True God, because he has True Divinity derived to him from the Father; whereas all False Gods, are no Gods at all: So God the Father is likewise, by way of Eminence, the One and Only Good, because He Alone is [ἀντομαγὴν] the original underived Fountain of Goodness; and yet Christ also is Truly Good, by having the Father's Goodness communicated to him without Measure; whereas False Gods, have neither Any Dominion, nor Any Goodness at all.

blocks.label: text
blocks.text: I reply: His affirming Self-originated and Begotten, to be, not essential, but personal Characters; is affirming, in other Words, that they are, not essential, but essential Characters. For What is a personal Character, but a Character which distinguishes That particular Person from all other Persons? and What is This, but the Essence of That Person? If we know any thing of the Essence of God, the first and of all others the most essential Character of him, is his being Self-existent or Unoriginated. The Substance of the Son, whatever the Nature of it be in other respects, yet is certainly derived from the Father; otherwise, the Son being Self-existent as well as the Father, it would follow, that Not the Person of the Son, (that is, Not the Son himself,) but the Personality only of the Son was begotten of the Father: Which is unintelligible Metaphysicks, and without any Foundation in Scripture. ROM. XI, 36. Of him, and through him, and to him are all things.
The Meaning (I think) is: From Him [viz. from the Father] all things derive their Being, by Him all things are preserved and governed, to his Glory all things shall terminate.
Your Learned Friend paraphrases the Words thus : Of him, as HE is Father; through him, as HE is Son ; to him (or rather, in him, for so the Particle es is frequently used,) as HE is the Holy Ghost.
Had he here intended to express the Sabellian Notion, which in the Whole amounts to the very same with Socinianism; denying the Son and Holy Ghost to be any thing more than mere empty Names; I know not how it could possibly have been declared in more full and expressive Words.

blocks.text: I observe one thing further upon This Head. Your Friend is very fond of confounding All Language. In the first Text he quotes, he will have [εις] to signify One Thing, instead of One Person. And here he would have [εις ἀστὴν] to signify, in Him, instead of, to Him: The Particle, he says, being Frequently so used. But there is no such thing in the World, as putting one Word, in this manner, for another: And indeed it is impossible there should; For, at that rate, no Language would have any Signification. Some Grammarians indeed give Instances of one Word's seeming to be put for another; But the Instances they allege, are always either Corruptions of the Copies, or else their own Mistakes. The like vulgar Error, with regard to the Particle [in] in the Latin Language, I have refuted in my Annotations upon Cafars Commentaries, ad lib. 4. de Bello Gallico, pag. 76, lin. 12. Sometimes indeed one and the same Word has indifferently two or more significations; and then it may (according as the Sense requires) be understood in Any of those Significations. Thus the Word [ἐπὶ] in the New Testament, according to the Genius of the Hebrew and Hellenistical Stile, signifies indifferently In or By. But there is no such thing in any Language, as putting one Word for another; And therefore εἰς ἀντον, (the Word εἰς having but one signification,) can be rendred no otherwise than To Him.

blocks.text: Your Friend alleges in the first place, that the general Design of the Epistle, is not to teach the Truth and Existence of the One only God, in opposition to Idols; but to encourage Believers to continue in the Faith of the Son of God, by assuring them that they had eternal Life by virtue of That Faith. And from hence he supposes the Apostle to conclude, that the Son of God, Jesus Christ, is Himself the True God, and the only way to Eternal Life, or rather Eternal Life itself; and that therefore Men ought to keep themselves from Idols, or from All Means of approaching God, besides this Divine Person.

blocks.text: In the next place, your Friend alleges, that the word [αλληδίνος, and οὐ αλληδίνος,] He that is True, is in St John's Writings seldom applied to the Father; in this first Epistle, never applied to the Father; but, in all his Writings, frequently applied to the Son: As Rev. 3, 7, These things faith He that is True; Rev. 3, 14, These things faith the Faithful and True Witness; & Rev. 19, 11, He that sat upon the white Horse, was called Faithful and True; as if, True, were a Name or Attribute more particularly the Son's. And from hence he infers, that therefore probably in the present passage also, the words, Him that is True, and, in Him that is True, and, the True God, are all spoken of the Son: Especially since, in the Construction of the words, [We are in Him that is True, even in his Son Jesus Christ,] 'tis plain (he says) that the Terms, in Him that is True, are explained by, in his Son; so that no doubt (he says) can be made, but that the word True belongs here to Christ; and therefore 'tis a strong Probability, that they are meant of Him also in the foregoing words, that we may know Him that is True.

And from hence he infers, that therefore probably in the present passage also, the words, Him that is True, and, in Him that is True, and, the True God, are all spoken of the Son: Especially since, in the Construction of the words, [We are in Him that is True, even in his Son Jesus Christ,] 'tis plain (he says) that the Terms, in Him that is True, are explained by, in his Son; so that no doubt (he says) can be made, but that the word True belongs here to Christ; and therefore 'tis a strong Probability, that they are meant of Him also in the foregoing words, that we may know Him that is True.
Now All this (which I have represented in its full force) is very plausible to an Unlearned Reader, and (I believe) very sincere

For it all depends upon Two very great Errours: One, an Error in the reading of the Original; The Other, a Mistake in the English Translation. The First, is an Error in the reading of the Original: For if your Friend had (as it was reasonable he should have done,) consulted Dr Mills; he would have found that the Most and Best Manuscripts have it, [ἐναγνωστὸν μεν τῆς αλληδίνον Θεόν,] that we may know [not, him that is True, but] the True GOD. Now though your Friend's Observation is very right, that [αλληδίνος, or ο αλληδίνος, he that is True,] when used alone, as Rev. 19, 11, always signifies the Son, because it is of the same import with [ο αλληδίνος μορφιws] the Faithful and True Witness, Rev. 3, 14: yet, on the contrary, when it is joined with [Θεός] God, it always signifies the Father, and never the Son: Job. 17, 3, That they might know Thee the Only True God [αλληδίνος θεόν,] and Jesus Christ whom thou hast sent; And I Th. 1, 9, To serve the Living and True God, [Θεώ αλληδίνος,] and to wait for His Son from Heaven. is True, were meant of Christ; Whom then would the word, His, refer to, in the following Period, even in HIS Son Jesus Christ? Is not, HIS Son, as much as to say, the Son [τὸ αλληγήν] of That True One? and if then by That True One was meant Christ, would not This be to say that Jesus Christ was the Son of Himself? Or, does the word, His, refer to some very remote Antecedent? The True Rendring therefore plainly is; that we may know the True God, and we are In That True God BY his Son Jesus Christ: That is; Christ has not only given us an Understanding to know and acknowledge the True God, but has moreover brought us to a still nearer Union and Communion with him, even so as to be In Him: Thus ch. 4, 15, Who soever shall confess that Jesus is the Son of God, God dwelleth in Him, and He in God; And John. 17, 21, Thou, Father, in Me, and I in Thee, that They also may be one in Us. The Design of the Apostle is not to prove (as your Friend supposes,) that we Are in Christ; but to infer from thence, (That being the Premise, not the Conclusion of his Argument,) that in like manner as Those who are in the World, (ver. 19,) are thereby [ἐν τὴν ποντηρ] in the Evil One, and, because they have not the Son, therefore neither have they the Father, ch. 2, 23; so We, on the contrary, who Are in Christ, are

Lastly, if any one shall allege, that the Præposition [ἐν,] repeated (as in this place) twice together in the same Sentence, cannot so vary, as in the one part to be rendred, in, and in the other, by; the following undeniable Instances will convince him of the contrary: Acts 7, 44, ἐν τοῖς παντεάσυν ἡμᾶν ἐν τὴν ερήνω, was with (or among) our Fathers in the Wilderness: Rom. 1, 9, ἐν τῆς συνεύματι μυεῦ τῆς ἐναγγελίω, with my Spirit, in the Gospel: Gal. 2, 20, ἐν σαρμι, ἐν πίστεα, in the Flesh, by the Faith: Ephes. 1, 3, ἐν παιση ευλογία ἐν τῆς επικεανιοις ἐν χειτώ, with all Blessings in Heavenly places in Christ: Ephes. 2, 6, ἐν τοῖς επικεανιος ἐν χειτώ, in Heavenly places in [with or by] Christ: Ephes. 3, 21, ἐν τῆς επικλεσις ἐν χειτώ, in the Church by Christ: 2 Th. 1, 4, ἐν υμιν ἐν ταῖς επικλεσις, in [concerning] you in the Churches: 1 Joh, 4, 9, ἐν τέτω—ἐν μμίν, in This—towards us. True God and Truly God, meaning thereby,
(as I have above shown at large, pag. 11,)
not Self-existent, Independent, Underived Divinity; but (as he expressly explains himself in the * Book your Friend so often refers to,) that Christ is Truly God, by having RECEIVED from his Father True Divinity and Dominion over the whole Creation; whereas False Gods have no Divinity or Dominion at all. But in what Sense soever Christ is by Irenaeus affirmed to be, and in reality is, True God; yet in This Text 'tis not He, that is spoken of by that Name. For the preceding Word, He that is True, (to which your Friend thinks nothing but Apparent Prejudice can hinder a Man from referring the following Words, This is the True God;) I say, the preceding Word, He that is True, being spoken (as I have now shown) not of the Son, (as your Friend supposes,) but of the Father; it follows plainly that the next Words, This is the True God, are meant also, not of the Son, but of the Father. For it cannot be, but the same Person must be spoken of throughout; that we may know the TRUE GOD, and we are in Him that is TRUE

True God and Truly God, meaning thereby,
(as I have above shown at large, pag. 11,)
not Self-existent, Independent, Underived Divinity; but (as he expressly explains himself in the * Book your Friend so often refers to,) that Christ is Truly God, by having RECEIVED from his Father True Divinity and Dominion over the whole Creation; whereas False Gods have no Divinity or Dominion at all. But in what Sense soever Christ is by Irenaeus affirmed to be, and in reality is, True God; yet in This Text 'tis not He, that is spoken of by that Name. For the preceding Word, He that is True, (to which your Friend thinks nothing but Apparent Prejudice can hinder a Man from referring the following Words, This is the True God;) I say, the preceding Word, He that is True, being spoken (as I have now shown) not of the Son, (as your Friend supposes,) but of the Father; it follows plainly that the next Words, This is the True God, are meant also, not of the Son, but of the Father. For it cannot be, but the same Person must be spoken of throughout; that we may know the TRUE GOD, and we are in Him that is TRUE

The word, [ἐπιος, This,] refers back, as is most natural and usual, not to the last word in Order, but to the last and principal in Sense, that which was uppermost in the Writers Thoughts, and chiefly aimed at in the Whole Discourse. Had St John intended to affirm, what your Friend supposes; he would not have said, ἐπιος εὐν, but 'Εὐσί ἐπιος, or ἐπισί μεχι ἐπιος &c. Neither would he have said, ἐπιος εὐν [ο] αλληλινος ἐπιος; for That would have been affirming the Person of the Son to be the very Person of the Father before mentioned; but he would have said, ἐπιος εὐν, or ἐπισί μεχι ἐπιος, 'Αλληλινος ἐπιος. For, as I before observed, though Θεος is often the same as ο θεος, yet, on the contrary, ο θεος is never by Any Writers put for Θεος: As the Learned well understand. It ought also to weigh somewhat with your Friend, that None of the Writers of the Three First Centuries allege these words, This is the True God, as spoken of Christ.

blocks.text: That the Terms, eternal Life, are indeed in this whole Epistle applied only to the Son, is very true; but This proves, not what your Friend supposes, but the contrary. For St John does not say, that The True God IS eternal Life; but he Therefore calls the Son eternal Life, because it is He that bringeth us to the True God. He is the Way, the Truth, and the Life; and is so, by giving us an Understanding (as this very Text expresses it) that we may know the True God. blocks.text: Your Friend wishes some Instances had been given, in which the True God is used for the True Religion. I answer: By the same Figure that Idols or False Gods, in the very next Words, signifie the Worship of False Gods, which is False Religion; by the very same figure of speaking here, the True God signifies the Worship of the True God, which is True Religion. 'Tis in Neither Case, a strict Translation; but in Both, a true Paraphrase.

blocks.text: cerned in the Generation of the Son, it will follow unavoidably that the Son was not generated at all from the Father, but was as much Self-existent as the Father himself. For whatever is caused by an Intelligent Being, is caused by the Will of That Being. Otherwise it is not (in Truth and Reality) caused by That Being at all, but by some Superior Cause, (be it Necessity, or Fate, or Whatever it be;) under which, the Intelligent Being is in such Case as much an Instrument only, as if it was wholly Unintelligent. For which Reason, All the Learnedest of the Orthodox Fathers, who understood how to argue closely and strongly; Justin Martyr, Origen, Novatian, Eusebius, the Council of Sirmium, Marius Victorinus, Basil, Gregory Nyssen, and indeed almost all Antient Writers excepting only Athanasius; professedly argue (as I have shown at large in my Scripture-doctrine, Part II, §. 17,) that the Son was generated of the Father, not by absolute Necessity of Nature, but by an Act of his eternal Power and Will. Which is the only intelligible Foundation of that Authority the Scripture every where ascribes to the Father in the Mission of the Son. And though the Scripture has no where indeed in express Terms, declared the Generation of the Son to be by the Will of the Father; yet it does so by plain Consequence, when

Not so in this place: For there is no mention of False Gods in the Context: But One God is put directly as the Person mediated to, (which all Men allow to be the Father only,) in contradistinction to the Person mediating to him, which is the Whole Person of the Son incarnate. Wherefore though the mentioning the Son here (as your Friend goes on) After the One God, had not in it self been a sufficient Argument that he is excluded out of the One God; yet the mentioning him with the Character of Mediatour, in contradistinction to the One God mentioned under the Character of the Person mediated to, evidently shows him to be not included here by the Apostle in Him whom He thus stiles by way of Eminence the One God.

blocks.text: Now from this whole passage, what any Man can infer contrary to any thing I have anywhere affirmed, I cannot imagine. Only instead of the words which We now read, Worship God, (that is, according to the general Use of the word God in the New Testament, worship the Father ;) Cyprian either read in his Copies, or perhaps cited by his Memory, the following words, Worship the Lord Jesus. Which, though not the True Reading of the Text, yet contains nothing in it inconsistent with what I said in my Scripture-doctrine concerning absolutely Supreme Worship being peculiar to the Person of the Father. For Most of those Fathers, in those very Passages he cites, explain themselves (as will appear immediately) in the very same manner as I have done. But your Friend, not content to understand these words in the Text, in the same Sense as the like words are found in his Quotations; labours to suggest another Sense, which yet he cares not to express distinctly, but leaves it darkly to his Reader to infer as well as he can. If his words infer any thing; it must

blocks.text: must be, that the Son is so stiled Lord God, as not to be distinguished from the Father: Which, when expressed intelligibly, can end in nothing else, (though your Friend seems not to intend it.) but in denying the Son to have Any Being at all: Which is the Socinian Notion. And What Need is there of interpreting Scripture after so unintelligible a manner, when All the Texts in their obvious and natural Sense carry with them another Signification? That which seems to have led your Friend into This, is a Notion he has entertained of certain Scripture-Interpretations justly Conceived to be founded upon TRADITION, and of certain Doctrines and Expositions of the Sacred Writings, handed down to the Fathers by TRADITION from Their Fathers. What and where this Tradition is, it does not appear: For the Greater Part of the Fathers plainly enough expresses the very Notion I am pleading for; (as the Reader will see presently in those very Passages, which your Friend has cited to prove the contrary:) But What that Doctrine is, which your Friend alludes to as Traditionary, remains very obscure; and he himself leaves it to his Reader to guess at, rather than any where explicitly expresses it. What he drops in different places, amounts (if any thing) to a Total Confusion of Persons: Which Persons he sometimes speaks of.

blocks.text: This, your Friend replies, that elsewhere $^S$ Thomas calls Christ, My Lord and my God. But I answer, This is plainly meant in That Sense, in which $^S$ Paul applies to him the Title God in that Citation out of the Psalmist; Thy Throne, O God, is for ever and ever; thou hast loved Righteousness; therefore GOD, even THY GOD, [or, therefore, O God, THY GOD] hath anointed thee, &c. Your Friend alleges but one Text more, Rev. 22, 6, The Lord God of the Holy Prophets sent his Angel: And this he thinks is meant of the Son, because it is said, Rev. 1, 1, that Jesus sent his Angel. As if it might not very properly be said, that God the Father sent That Angel, whom Christ sent forth with that Revelation which God the Father gave him to send by the Angel. There are in Scripture innumerable Instances of the like manner of speaking. And that the Lord God of the Holy Prophets does indeed here signify the Father, is evident from hence, that, in the five fore-going Verses of the same Chapter, the word, God, and Lord God, are used two or three times in express contradiction to the Lamb.

But does St John indeed use the Word, God (not only sometimes for the Father, and sometimes for the Son, but also) for Both Together? Verily, had your Friend considered here what he said, I am perswaded he would not have stood to it. For observe what a Paraphrase his Criticism makes, when applied to the Text he directs us to apply it to. John, I, 1. The Word was with God, and the Word was God; that is, The Word was with the Father and the Son, and the Word was the Father and the Son. This is no misrepresentation of his Sense; but is his True, real, and professed Meaning. blocks.text: tue of their Names invoked in Baptism, begets us into Children, so that we are the Sons of Both Persons. By This Argument he should have said, we are the Sons of the Three Persons. But the Scripture gives quite a different Account of this Matter. We are There called The Sons of God, because we are made, in our measure and degree, by Adoption and Grace, what Christ was, in a complete and perfect manner, by Nature: We are represented as Heirs of God, and Joint-Heirs with Christ, that is, Brethren of Christ and Sons of God. If then our being Sons of God, means that we are Sons of the Father and the Son; then also Christ's being the Son of God, means that he is the Son of the Father and the Son. When once Confusion is introduced, there is no End of Absurdities. But your Friend draws one Argument more, from the Word [φανεωρὸν he shall appear,] used in the next verse, 1 John, 3, 2. Now are we the Sons of God, (that is, faith be, of the One God, Father and Son:) But when He shall appear, (that is, faith be, when the One God shall appear in the Person of the Son.) Put now these two Explications together, and then the whole verse stands thus: Now are we the Sons of the Father and the Son; But when the Father and the Son shall appear in the Person of the Son, we shall be like HIM.

To This, our Saviour replies, ver. 17, My Father worketh hitherto, and I work: That is to say; Though the works of God are finished from the Foundation of the World, and my Father ceased indeed on the Seventh day from his works of Creation; yet his works of Providence and Goodness go on every day for ever without Intermission; and I likewise do works of Goodness and Charity, even on the Sabbath-day. The Jews, willing to take any handle (though never so unreasonable) of Accusing him, infer, ver. 18, (by way of Calumny, not by way of strict Reasoning,) that his calling God his Father [o πατρὰ μυ] was as much as assuming to Himself, that God who was the common Father of them All, was in a higher and more peculiar manner [πατρὰ ιδιον]

Exod. 23, 21, and Acts 7, 30,] cannot be approved of: But if it be intended to show, that the Angel or Christ is a distinct Subject or substantially different from the Name of God in him, not in respect of his Divine Nature, but of a Created Nature assumed by the Word at the beginning of all things, as the First-fruits of the Creation, and in respect of which He may be more properly and accurately denominated an Angel; it may be readily assented to, as a strong Probability, not a little favoured by the Sacred Writings.

blocks.text: of an Unity of Nature : Not by considering the Context, and the Connexion of the words ; but by Two foreign Arguments. The first, is ; that the Name of God, [Jehovah,] is in several places of Scripture given to the Son: And in what manner This is done, I have just now explained, in the fore-going No 24. The second Argument is, a Collection of Sentences out of the Fathers: Some of which, do not at all mean what your Friend thinks of; (especially those of Novatian; As the Reader will find by comparing the Passages themselves with what immediately goes before and follows after, and with the other Passages which I have above cited out of the same Author :) And the Rest are no Proofs at all, what is the True Meaning of the Texts now before us.

This appears plainly, from the Answer our Lord gave them in the words immediately following, ver. 34, 35, 36, Is it not written in your Law, I said, ye [Rulers and Magistrates] are Gods, [and Children of the most High?] If he called Them Gods, unto whom the word of God came, and the Scripture cannot be broken; Say ye of Him whom the Father bath sanctified and sent into the World, Thou blasphemeest, because I said, I AM THE SON OF GOD? From these words 'tis evident, that their Charge against him of Blasphemy, for which they went about to Stone him, was founded upon his calling God his Father, (see above, in No. 23,) or declaring himself to be the Son of God; which they, in their Anger, represented, by way of Aggravation, as making himself God.

Thy Sins be forgiven thee; they answer, Why doth this Man thus speak Blasphemies? Who can forgive Sins, but God only? The Blasphemy they accuse him of here, was his taking upon himself, not the Person, but the Power and Authority of God, to forgive Sins. Again; when he was brought before Pilate, the Accusation against him was, Job. 19, 7, We have a Law, and by our Law he ought to die, because he made himself the Son of God. What they understood here by his making himself the Son of God, and thereby being guilty of Blasphemy; appears from the Account given in the other Three Gospels, of his Examination before the High-Priest in the Council. St Matt. 26, 63, Tell us (said the High-Priest) whether thou be the Christ the Son of God: Jesus faith unto him, Thou hast said: [ἐν λέγειω] not, Nevertheless; but, Moreover] I say unto you, Hereafter shall ye see the Son of Man sitting on the right-hand of Power, and coming in the Clouds of Heaven: Then the High-Priest rent his Clothes, saying, He bath spoken Blasphemy,——ye have heard his Blasphemy. St Mark relates it thus; ch. 14, 61, Art thou the Christ, the Son of the Blessed? And Jesus said, I am; And ye shall see the Son of Man sitting on the right-hand. &c. St Luke thus; ch. 22, 67, They asked him, saying, Art thou the Christ? He answered,

Again; when he was brought before Pilate, the Accusation against him was, Job. 19, 7, We have a Law, and by our Law he ought to die, because he made himself the Son of God. What they understood here by his making himself the Son of God, and thereby being guilty of Blasphemy; appears from the Account given in the other Three Gospels, of his Examination before the High-Priest in the Council. St Matt. 26, 63, Tell us (said the High-Priest) whether thou be the Christ the Son of God: Jesus faith unto him, Thou hast said: [ἐν λέγειω] not, Nevertheless; but, Moreover] I say unto you, Hereafter shall ye see the Son of Man sitting on the right-hand of Power, and coming in the Clouds of Heaven: Then the High-Priest rent his Clothes, saying, He bath spoken Blasphemy,——ye have heard his Blasphemy. St Mark relates it thus; ch. 14, 61, Art thou the Christ, the Son of the Blessed? And Jesus said, I am; And ye shall see the Son of Man sitting on the right-hand. &c. St Luke thus; ch. 22, 67, They asked him, saying, Art thou the Christ? He answered,

blocks.text: De ovibus etiam suis, quod nemo illas de manu ejus eriperet. Pater enim quod mihi dedit, majus est omnibus ; &, Ego for Pater Unum sumus. — Unum sumus, non, Unus sumus. — Unum dicit, neutrali verbo; qued non pertinet ad Singularitatem, sed ad Unitatem, ad Similitudinem, ad Conjunctionem; ad Dilectionem Patris, qui Filium diligit; & ad obsequium Filii, qui voluntati Patris obsequitur. Unum sumus, dicens, Ego for Pater; ostendit duos esse, quos aquat & jungit. Adeo addit etiam mulra se opera a Patre ostendisse, quorum nihil lapidari mereretur. Et ne putarent ideo se illum lapidare debere, quasi se Deum ipsum, id est Patrem, voluisset intelligi; quia djxerat, Ego for Pater Unum sumus; qua Filium Dei Deum ostendens, non qua iplum Deum : Si in lege, inquit, scriptum est, Ego dixi, vos diii estis; & non potest be.

blocks.text: solvi Scriptura; quem Pater sanctificavit, & misit in mundum, vos eum blasphemare dicitis, quia dixi, Filius Dei sum? Si non facio opera Patris mei, nolite credere; si vero facio, & Mihi credere non vultis, vel propter opera credite: Et scirote qudd ego in Patre sim, & Pater in Me. Per opera ergo erat pater in filio, & filius in Patre; & ita per opera intelligimus Unum esse Patrem & Filium. Adeo totum hoc perseverabat inducere, ut duo tamen crederentur in una virtute; quia aliter Filius credi non posset, nifi duo crederentur. Adverf.Praxeam. c. 22.

Thus also Novatian: If Christ (faith he) had been the Father, as the Hereticks imagine; he would have said, I and my Father Am One, [Unus, One Person.] But One, in the Neuter Gender, [Unum, One Thing,] signifies Agreement of Fellowship, not Unity of Person. So that the Father and Son are One Thing, by Agreement and Love. The Apostle Paul also takes notice of this Unity of
Agreement, with a Difference of Persons. He that planteth, faith be, and he that watereth, are One, [One Thing.] Now every body knows, that yet Apollos was One Man, and Paul another, and not Paul and Apollos One and the Same Man.

him to be o' œv, it will prove him to be, not only the same individual Being, but also the same individual Person with the Father. Which is more than your Friend intended to infer. And therefore the Son's being True God, must not be understood to signify that he is o' œv, but that He has True Divinity (which False Gods have not,) communicated to him from Him who is Alone o' œv. But your Friend proceeds:

"Since (faith be) the One True God is but One individual Being; and the Father is This One True God; the Son, if he is a distinct individual Being from the Father, must be distinct from the One True God, that is, be no True God himself at all; Which is contrary to 1 John. 5, 20". (And This also is Dr Wells's chief Argument: Letter to Dr Clarke, pag. 59.) I answer: That passage of St John, is not spoken of the Son; as I have shown above, No 14. But if it was, still it would follow, that the Son was True God, not by being himself the Father, the Self-existent Being; but by having True Divinity and Dominion communicated to him from Him, as I before said.

blocks.text: What he further offers upon this Head, (pag. 79;) that the Name Jehovah, or the Divine Virtue of the Name, did not lodge in the Word, as in a distinct Subject, but was the very Word itself; That (pag. 81,) the Son revealing the Father, is the very Name, and not the bare Subject in which it dwells; That (pag. 82,) since the Apostle tells us there is none other Name under Heaven (but the Name of Jesus Christ) given among Men, whereby we must be saved; and it is certain the Name by which the Church is to be saved according to the Prophecies of the Old Testament, is the Name Jehovah; it follows therefore that the Name Jesus, and the Name Jehovah, are One: All This, is to Me utterly unintelligible.

The Son manifesting the Father, is (he says) the same Object of Divine Worship to the Christians, as God the Creator was to the Gentiles: —Otherwise the Christians in their New Dispensation, which is a plain Improvement of the State of Nature, would have a Name to trust in, of lesser Efficacy, than the very Gentiles. As if Christians did not trust in God the Father, the Creator of all things; as well as the Gentiles, who knew him much more imperfectly; Besides that Christians have moreover, (whom the Gentiles knew not,) an Advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous, who is their Saviour, Redeemer, and Intercessor.

blocks.text: Lastly, he sums up his Argument, (pag. 82;) Therefore the Son manifesting the Father, is One with God the Creator, since the True God is but One: And (pag. 83,) If then Jehovah be incommunicable to any but the True God, and the True God is but One, and Jesus Christ is Jehovah; Jesus Christ is the True God. Your learned Friend alleges, that, not only God will judge the World by Jesus Christ, but Jesus Christ himself also is both Lord and God. I acknowledge, and have shown at large, that he is so. But your Friend, not content with This, laboureth further to introduce an unaccountable Confusion of Persons; by arguing, that when St Paul says, ver. 6, He that eateth, eateth to the Lord, and giveth God thanks; and He that eateth not, to the Lord he eateth not, and giveth God thanks; it Seems, and it is Reasonable (he thinks) to Suppose, that the word, God, in each of these Sentences, signifies Christ. But This is so directly contrary to the whole Style of the New Testament, that he is not very Consident of his Assertion: And therefore he tells us it is yet more probable, if we consider, that when St Paul faith of a weak Brother, ver. $^{3}$ of this Chapter, God has received him; he afterwards expresses the same thing thus, ch. 15, 7, Christ also has received us to the Glory of God; "putting Christ (says your Friend) in the place of God, as if He were comprehended in that Name". Your learned Friend alleges, that, not only God will judge the World by Jesus Christ, but Jesus Christ himself also is both Lord and God. I acknowledge, and have shown at large, that he is so. But your Friend, not content with This, laboureth further to introduce an unaccountable Confusion of Persons; by arguing, that when St Paul says, ver. 6, He that eateth, eateth to the Lord, and giveth God thanks; and He that eateth not, to the Lord he eateth not, and giveth God thanks; it Seems, and it is Reasonable (he thinks) to Suppose, that the word, God, in each of these Sentences, signifies Christ. But This is so directly contrary to the whole Style of the New Testament, that he is not very Confident of his Assertion: And therefore he tells us it is yet more probable, if we consider, that when St Paul faith of a weak Brother, ver. $^{3}$ of this Chapter, God has received him; he afterwards expresses the same thing thus, ch. 15, 7, Christ also has received us to the Glory of God; "putting Christ (says your "Friend) in the place of God, as if He "were comprehended in that Name". blocks.label: text
blocks.text: Of the Two Arguments your Learned Friend alleges for understanding these words concerning the Person of Christ, the first is the Context or Connexion of the words. The Apostle in the preceding Verse, encourages Christians to imitate their own Pastors in the Constancy of their Faith; the Object of which was Jesus Christ, who was no Person of a modern Date, but the same Yesterday, and to day, and for ever. Thus your Learned Friend. But Where now is the Force of This Argument? Imitate your own Pastors, because the Person of Christ is always the same. The Context, I think, plainly shows the other to be the True Sense: Adhere to the Faith of the Apostles who first instructed you, and be not carried about with divers new Doctrines; For the Doctrine of Christ is always One and the same,

blocks.text: His Comment upon it, is nothing but an Inquiry, in eight very dark and obscure Pages, what the particular Manner was of Christ's devesting himself of his former Glory. The Circumstances whereof not being revealed to us, 'tis in vain to indeavour to explain them by Philosophical Conjectures, and uncertain Metaphysical Speculations. Sufficient it is, that the Thing itself is revealed very clearly and intelligibly; that That Divine Person, who had before appeared as Lord of All, exercising the Dominion of the Invisible Father, and being thereby in the Form of God; in the fulness of time condececended, in Obedience to the Good Pleasure of his Father, and with his own Free Will and Consent, to take upon him our Humane Flesh, and appear for our fakes in the Form of a Servant, as a Man of like Infirmities with Other Men, mean and humble and subjected even to Death.

Your Learned Friend joins these two Notions together; making that which is literal, to be at the same time figurative; and that which is only figurative, to be at the same time literal also: Which is a manifest Confusion and Impossibility. The latter of the Two Notions I now mentioned, is (I think) the more agreeable to the New Testament.

blocks.text: Testament. The Son of God is That Divine Person, by whom the Wisdom of the Father is manifested, and his Will revealed to all his Creatures; And upon That Account (as I observed,) His Name (says the Scripture) is called The WORD of God, ἀγλείτην ὑνομας ἄπτῶν, ὁ λόγος τὸ θεῶν, Rev. 19, 13. And if the Gospel of St John was written after the Revelation, (as is not improbable;) then the Reason of Christ's being called The Word, or That Word, in the first Verse of that Gospel, is the same with regard to this passage in the Revelation; as his being so frequently stiled in the Gospels, The Son of Man, or That Son of Man, is with regard to the person so stiled and described in the prophecy of Daniel, ch. 7, 13. Now because the word [λόγος] happens also to signify, Reason; hence the Authors your Friend cites, conclude, that Christ is literally the Reason or Wisdom of the Father; and, by Consequence, no Person at all. There are several other Passages in the New Testament, wherein Christ is called likewise the Power and the Righteousness of God: Very elegantly and emphatically; because by Him is manifested the Power, and by him is set forth in a most conspicuous manner The Righteousness [διαγγοσυν, πρυχ, The Mercy] of the Father. From hence the same Authors might have argued.

blocks.label: text
blocks.text: Your learned Friend says not a word upon this Text; but only unfortunately cites one passage out of Irenæus, upon which he makes a wrong Observation. Requiescebat Spiritus Dei super Eum; The Spirit of God (faith Irenæus) rested upon him, viz. upon Christ. "EUM, (says "your Learned Friend,) the Man, not the "Word". He had forgot, it seems, that he was citing a Latin Translation; and that Irenæus wrote in Greek, in which Both the words [λῶν and αὐτῶντος] are equally Masculine. But This is of no great Moment: For in the whole passage, he does indeed represent Irenæus's Sense rightly; though he mistook in judging where the Emphasis of the Expresfion lay.

blocks.text: The Texts in the second and third Chapters of the Revelation, where the words of Christ are said to be what the Spirit faith unto the Churches, are thus explained by your Friend: Because (faith he) the One Glory of the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost, was manifested in the Humane Nature of Christ, though the Word only was personally united to it; are the words of Christ attributed to the Spirit. To Me, the Reason of This Expression [what the SPIRIT faith unto the Churches,] seems rather to be This; that 'twas by being in the Spirit, (ch. 1, 10,) 'twas by the Inspiration of the Spirit, that St John saw That Vision, wherein Christ was represented as speaking to him those words. Which of these two Interpretations is the more reasonable and intelligible, must be left to the Reader to judge.

blocks.label: text
blocks.text: He goes on therefore to another Argument : If Any Crime is unpardonable, Blasphemy doubtless against the God of Heaven, or the Person of the Father, is so ; as being an Act of open Defiance and most provoking Insolence. I answer : Though no Crime is, in its own Nature, greater than Blasphemy against God ; yet a Crime may, upon account of certain Circumstances, become more unpardonable, as being more remote from Repentance. Of This Kind is Blaspheming the Greatest and Last Means of Conviction ; ascribing the most beneficial , as well as most powerful Works, to an unclean Spirit ; and thereby taking away all possible means of distinguishing Good from Evil : Which therefore our Saviour does accordingly in express Words here declare to be more unpardonable than Any other Blasphemy whatsoever.

He goes on therefore to another Argument : If Any Crime is unpardonable, Blasphemy doubtless against the God of Heaven, or the Person of the Father, is so ; as being an Act of open Defiance and most provoking Insolence. I answer : Though no Crime is, in its own Nature, greater than Blasphemy against God ; yet a Crime may, upon account of certain Circumstances, become more unpardonable, as being more remote from Repentance. Of This Kind is Blaspheming the Greatest and Last Means of Conviction ; ascribing the most beneficial , as well as most powerful Works, to an unclean Spirit ; and thereby taking away all possible means of distinguishing Good from Evil : Which therefore our Saviour does accordingly in express Words here declare to be more unpardonable than Any other Blasphemy whatsoever.

the Spirit of the Living God; not in Tables of Stone, but in fleshy Tables of the Heart: That is; The Power and Efficacy of the Gospel, is as much greater than that of the Law, as can be expresst by comparing that which is written in a Book, with that which is imprinted inwardly in the very Heart and Soul itself. The same Argument he pursues, ver. 6, God hath made us able Ministers of the New Testament, not of the Letter, but of the Spirit; for the Letter killeth, but the Spirit giveth Life: That is; The Gospel gives us those Spiritual Precepts, whereof the Legal Ordinances were but Types and Shadows; and teaches us the way to eternal Life, whereas the Rigour of the Law could end only in Mens condemnation. And from hence he proceeds to magnify the glorious Manifestation of the Gospel, by comparing it with the Glory that shined in Moses's Countenance; which, though so bright that the Children of Israel could not stedfastly behold it, yet was but temporary and transient, and only a Type or Figure of That permanent Glory of the Gospel, which was to continue for ever: Ver. 7. blocks.text: Spirit be rather glorious For if the Ministration of Condemnation be Glory, much more doth the Ministration of Righteousness, (of Fussification, it should be rendred,) exceed in Glory:——For if That which was done away was glorious, much more That which remaineth (that which is Perpetual) is glorious. And hereupon he takes occasion elegantly to describe the Blindness of the Jews after our Saviour's time, in not seeing through the Types and Figures of the Old Testament; by comparing it to the Veil which Moses put upon his Face to conceal the Brightness of it: Ver. 14, 15, 16, Their Minds (faith he) were blinded; For until this day remaineth the same Veil untaken away, in the reading of the Old Testament; which Veil is done away in Christ: But even unto this day, when Moses is read, the Veil is upon their Heart: Nevertheless when it [when the Heart of the People of the Jews] shall turn to the Lord [shall be converted to Christ.] the Veil shall be taken away: As he had said just before, ver. 14, which Veil is done away in Christ.

blocks.text: of This different Signification. In One place, the Word, which we render, Glass, signifies a Perspective-glass, [βλέπομεν διεσπίλρει] which brings distant things into the Reach indeed of our Sight, but still very obscurely, imperfectly, and indistinctly; and does therefore very elegantly, and by a most proper Similitude, express That View of a Future State, which we have by Faith and not by Sight. But now in This Other place, the Word which we render, Glass, [κατοωιλειζόμενοι] signifies a Mirroir or Looking-glass, which on the contrary represents things plainly and distinctly, Face to Face; and therefore no less elegantly represents that clear Light of the Knowledge of the Glory and Will of God, which shines to us (faith the Apostle) in the FACE of Jesus Christ.

In One place, the Word, which we render, Glass, signifies a Perspective-glass, [βλέπομεν διεσπίλρει] which brings distant things into the Reach indeed of our Sight, but still very obscurely, imperfectly, and indistinctly; and does therefore very elegantly, and by a most proper Similitude, express That View of a Future State, which we have by Faith and not by Sight. But now in This Other place, the Word which we render, Glass, [κατοωιλειζόμενοι] signifies a Mirroir or Looking-glass, which on the contrary represents things plainly and distinctly, Face to Face; and therefore no less elegantly represents that clear Light of the Knowledge of the Glory and Will of God, which shines to us (faith the Apostle) in the FACE of Jesus Christ.

Lastly; Were there no other Argument, it would be sufficient to allege, that your Friends understanding the word, Lord, in this place, to mean the Holy Ghost; is entirely contrary to the whole Language of the inspired Writings, and tends to introduce the utmost confusion. For neither in the Old, nor in the New Testament, is there any one place, where the Holy Ghost is ever spoken of under the Title of Lord, but always distinctly under his own proper personal Denomination, the Spirit of the Lord, or the Spirit of God, or the Holy Spirit. There are only Two Places (and those your Friend seems not to have been aware of,) wherein Basil, contrary to all the Writers in the Ages before him, understands the word, Lord, to mean the Holy Ghost. Which Testimony of the Apostle St John, the Blessed Cyprian Bishop of Carthage, and Martyr, in his Epistle or Book which he wrote concerning the Trinity,

blocks.text: ANSW. It is easy to demonstrate, that this Suggestion is by no means reasonable or well-grounded. The Body of Christians in the Primitive Ages, kept stedfast to that Form of Sound Words, the Baptistical Creed; which contained nothing in it, but what both Arians, and almost all other Seets whatsoever, were forced to acknowledge was the true and undoubted Doctrine of Christ: Is it from hence reasonable to suggest, that the Christian Church in the Primitive Ages was justly to be ranked under Some Arian Clafs, or under any Clafs of any other Seet whatsoever? This Learned Author will not suspect that it was. He therefore only is an Arian, who himself maintains, or imposes upon others, the particular Doctrines of Arius; Not he, who desires to adhere to those Antient and Scriptural Forms of Sound Words, which being from the Beginning unanimously received in the Catholick Church, had afterwards different Additions made to them by Men of different Seets and different Opinions, whereby endless Disputes were brought into the Church.

Now to say, that besides the One True God, there cannot be also One True Lord or Mediatour; is an Argument, not against my Scheme in particular; but 'tis the Argument which Deists use, (with what reason, I have elsewhere shown,) against Christianity in general. Or to say, that there is also indeed One True Lord or Mediatour, but that That One True Lord is the same Individual with the One True God; What is This, but to affirm in other words, that the One Lord, Jesus Christ, B T whom are all things, is the One God, the Father, O F whom are all things? Which is overturning the Apostles whole Argument, and introducing an absolute Confusion of Persons. Our One God, says the Apostle, is the Father: If then the One Lord, Jesus Christ, be That One God, whom the Apostle defines to be the Father, of whom are all things; is not this expressly affirming that the Son is the Father? Than which, nothing can be more hard to understand, or to reconcile with the whole Doctrine of Scripture.

One God, to whom Mediation is made; and One Mediatour, making Intercession for us to That One God, (which is St Paul's manner of speaking;) are no more Two Gods; than an Advocate with the Father, and the Father with whom that Advocate is, (which is St John's manner of expressing the same thing;) are Two Fathers. One Spirit, One Lord, One God and Father of all, who is above all; are by the Apostle represented to us, as Three distinct Agents: And yet they can no more truly be said to be Three Gods, than Each of them singly, (or than All of them together;) can be truly said to be The God and Father of All, who is Above All; Which is the Apostles Definition of the One Supreme God. blocks.text: pag. 11. OBf. ' There can be no middle Beings, between the Creator, and the Creature.

paragraphs.text: pag. 11. OBf. ' There can be no middle Beings, between the Creator, and the Creature.

blocks.label: text
blocks.text: ANSW. This, if it be true, proves evidently the impossibility of this learned Writers own Scheme. For, the Creator signifying (in Scripture-phrase) the Father of all things, who created all things by his Son; if now there cannot possibly be any thing between the Supreme Father of All things, and That System of Beings which we call The Creature; it will of Necessity follow, that the Son of God must be either the Supreme Father himself, or else a mere Creature. To avoid this consequence, he is forced to suppose (pag. 129,) that the Son is something more than a mere Name, and yet not a real distinct Being; that is to say, that he is something between a Being and not a Being: Which is an undeniable Contradiction. I cannot but wonder, so learned a Writer should complain of My Scheme, for being what, after the most diligent Perusal, he cannot fully comprehend; and at the same time set up One in opposition to it, which of Necessity terminates either in a manifest Contradiction, or else in a Doctrine which of all others has always been esteemed the most Heterodox.

blocks.text: Powers or Attributes. Self-existence therefore is a primary, nay The primary and most essential Attribute of the Divine Substance. The Knowledge and Power of God, are not properly said to be Self-existent, but to be Attributes of Him who is himself Self-existent. The reason why the individual Knowledge or Power of God, cannot be communicated any more than his individual Existence, is because they are individual; and nothing that is individual, can ever be communicated from any one thing to another. Could the individual Knowledge of God, or the individual Knowledge of a Man, be communicated to another; there would be no Knowledge left in Him, from whom it was communicated. But the World well understands what is meant by Communication of Knowledge, Power, and the like: Could this learned Writer show as well how Self-existent Nature [or The Self-existent Nature] can be communicated, without an express Contradiction; this would be of great importance to him indeed.

The Knowledge and Power of God, are not properly said to be Self-existent, but to be Attributes of Him who is himself Self-existent. The reason why the individual Knowledge or Power of God, cannot be communicated any more than his individual Existence, is because they are individual; and nothing that is individual, can ever be communicated from any one thing to another. Could the individual Knowledge of God, or the individual Knowledge of a Man, be communicated to another; there would be no Knowledge left in Him, from whom it was communicated. But the World well understands what is meant by Communication of Knowledge, Power, and the like: Could this learned Writer show as well how Self-existent Nature [or The Self-existent Nature] can be communicated, without an express Contradiction; this would be of great importance to him indeed.
