blocks.text: But now on the other side, where the Word God is by the Construction necessarily determined to signify either two Persons or three, there is no one Text to be found. Which then of these Two, is begging the Question? To suppose that the Word God, when it occurs absolutely, is to be understood in the Same Sense, wherein it is acknowledged that of necessity it must by the Construction of the Text itself be understood in more than 300 other places of the same Book? Or, to understand it in a Sense, wherein there cannot be shown to be any Ground for understanding it in Any One Text? Besides: if the Word God, which always signifies an Intelligent and Powerful Agent, were ever made use of in Scripture to signifie what this Learned Author calls the Divine Nature, viz. the whole Three Persons, who are each of them also in Scripture always spoken of as Intelligent Agents; it would follow unavoidably, that the Divine Nature was a Fourth Intelligent Agent, distinct from, and constituted of, those Three Intelligent Agents. Which is the utmost Confusion imaginable.

But now on the other side, where the Word God is by the Construction necessarily determined to signify either two Persons or three, there is no one Text to be found. Which then of these Two, is begging the Question? To suppose that the Word God, when it occurs absolutely, is to be understood in the Same Sense, wherein it is acknowledged that of necessity it must by the Construction of the Text itself be understood in more than 300 other places of the same Book? Or, to understand it in a Sense, wherein there cannot be shown to be any Ground for understanding it in Any One Text? Besides: if the Word God, which always signifies an Intelligent and Powerful Agent, were ever made use of in Scripture to signifie what this Learned Author calls the Divine Nature, viz. the whole Three Persons, who are each of them also in Scripture always spoken of as Intelligent Agents; it would follow unavoidably, that the Divine Nature was a Fourth Intelligent Agent, distinct from, and constituted of, those Three Intelligent Agents. Which is the utmost Confusion imaginable.

blocks.text: ANSW. The Creation of a Human Soul, before the Creation of the World, before the Creation of Human Kind; is a mere Fiction without any Ground. A Human Soul formed more perfect than Any Angel, is a Human Soul created of a Higher Species than Human. The Notion itself, if it is at all intelligible, is perfectly the Arian Notion: The only difference is, that That which the Arians call a most excellent Created Spirit, is here stiled, much more improperly, a Human Soul. And to say we have no distinct Notion of any Perfections BETWEEN those which belong to GOD, and those which he hath imparted to MAN; is an Objection which (I humbly presume) needs no Answer.

And if so; then the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, was not the Son; unless the Son was the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ: Neither was the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, the whole Three Persons; unless the whole Three Persons were the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ. 'Tis True, the Person which appeared visibly to the Patriarchs, representing the invisible God and Father of All, was the Son: But then he is therefore called, both in the Old Testament and in the New, the ANGEL of the Lord: And in Him appeared the Glory of The Invisible God, whom the Patriarchs worshipped. blocks.text: But indeed in None of these places does the Word God mean Christ, but the Father, according to the Analogy of the whole New Testament, as I have shown at large in my Scripture-doctrine. Neither do any of these things belong to Christ in the Old Testament, any otherwise than as he was the Angel of his Father's Presence, the Visible Person that there represented the Invisible God. And particularly in that Passage, Heb. ii, 3, The Worlds were framed by the Word of GOD, it is manifestly absurd to affirm (as this learned Writer does) that the Word [God] means Christ. For then the Apostles Assertion would be This, The Worlds were framed by the Word of the WORD.: Whereas indeed, in That place, not the Word [God], but the Phrase [The Word of God,] signifies Christ.

blocks.text: Offices and Relation towards Us. Blessing and Honour is given unto Him that sitteth upon the Throne, [viz. to the Father,] upon account of his being θεός οὐσαντοκράτηρ, the Lord God Supreme Ruler over all: But unto the Lamb, standing in the midst of,[or before the midst of] the Throne, Glory is given upon account of his having loved us and washed us from our Sins in his own Blood, having redeemed us to God by his Blood, and made us unto our God Kings and Priests. The Glory given to the Son, is never founded upon such a Confusion of Persons, as this Learned Author every where supposes; but upon his being our Mediator and Advocate with the Father, and having a Name given him which is above every Name. And the reason our Saviour himself expressly gives, why he is to be honoured, as the Father is honoured; is, because the Father hath COMMITTED all judgment unto him, Joh. 5; 22, 23.

blocks.text: Almighty Himself. Wherein this Opinion really differs from that of our Learned Author himself, is (as I now observed) very hard to show. But that it was not the Opinion of the greatest part of Christians, those plain and unlearned Christians in Tertullian's time, who perpetually cried out, [Monarchiam tenemus,] We contend for the Government of One God over the Universe; appears from hence, that Tertullian calls Praxeas's Opinion [novellitatem Praxeae hefterni] a Novelty of Yesterday; whereas the Opinion of the then greater part of Christians, was what he supposes to prevail always among the unlearned, from the Simplicity of the Creed itself which taught them to believe in One God; [Simplices quique, quæ major temper credentium pars est; quoniam & ipsa REGULA Fidei a pluribus Diis seculi, ad Unicum & verum Deum transfert.] What this Opinion was, appears clearly enough in the Writers before and about that Time; viz. Justin, Irenæus, Origen and Novatian.

blocks.text: ANSW. Christ is never stiled either Supreme over all, or absolutely Supreme over all. He is indeed over All, and Lord of all; but still always excepting (as St Paul directs us) Him that did put all things under him. Supremacy therefore, is an Attribute of the Father, absolutely incommunicable. And to say, that, taking away the Distinctions of Father and Son, Christ is Supreme Lord of the Universe; is only saying in other words, that the Distinction between the Father and the Son is inconsiderable and to be neglected, because the Son also is Supreme, excepting only that he is not Supreme.

It should here have been added, by the very same reason; that the Son is also the Father of All, the One God and Father of All: And then the Force of the Argument, would have been evident to every Reader. The Truth of the matter, is plainly This: The word, God, when used absolutely, always signifies the Father: I cited, in that second Section which this Learned Author here refers to, more than three Hundred Texts, wherein the Construction of the words necessarily and confessedly determines it so to signify. But the Case is not so. There are, in all, thirteen Texts, wherein the word God has by some been thought to signify the Son;

Matt. 1, 23; Job. 10, 33; 20, 28; Aetys 20, 28; Rom. 9, 5; & 1 Tim. 3, 16;] are justly contested as ambiguous: That is to say; Either it is ambiguous whether the Word [θεὶς, God,] was originally in the Text at all; as Aetys 20, 28; Rom. 9, 5; & 1 Tim. 3, 16; Or else it is ambiguous whether it refers to the Father or the Son; and, if it refers to the Son, yet it is then clearly understood in a sense different from what this Learned Author supposes; as in the Three last-cited Texts, and in Matt. 1, 23; Job. 10, 33; & Job. 20, 28. Further: 'Tis worth observing upon this occasion, that not only θεότητα, the Divinity, or Supreme Dominion, of God; but even This other Word itself, θεοὺς God, has in Scripture, and in all Books of Morality and Religion, a relative Signification; and not, as in metaphysical Books, an Absolute One. As is evident from the relative Terms, which in moral Writings may always be joined with it. For instance: In the same manner as we say, my Father, my King, and the like; so it is proper also to say, my God, the God of Israel, the God of the Universe, and the like: Which Words are expressive of Dominion and Government. But, in the metaphysical way, it cannot be said, My Infinite Substance, The Infinite Substance of Israel, or the like. Which plainly shows in what Sense the Word Godhead, always ought to be understood in Theological Matters.

blocks.text: ed Author, (though his Interpretation necessarily infers it, yet) cares not to affirm. As to the critical Distinction between εἰς and εἴν, the Truth is evidently This. Because every Person is a Being, but every Being is not a Person; therefore εἰς, which is of the more limited Signification, and expresses intelligent Being or Person only, can never possibly be extended to signify Being in general: But εἴν, which signifies Being in general, may also be used of such a Being, as is an intelligent Being, that is, a Person. Therefore πὸ γεννησέν and πὸ αγον might properly be used by St Matthew and St Luke, as well as οὐαγωγο and οὐγεννησείς; because the Subject mentioned, (besides that perhaps πὸ πασιδίου is referred to), was equally both a Holy Thing and a Holy Person. But εἴν, in this place of St John, cannot signify One Being; because the Subject spoken of, being an Intelligent Being, it would consequently have meant the same as εἰς One Person: Which confessedly not being our Saviours intention to affirm, it follows of Necessity that the words must be understood figuratively, in the manner that has been above explained at large, pag. 144, ἀνc.

blocks.label: text
blocks.text: ANSW. Two Men are individually distinct from one another, not because they are finite, not because they are temporary, nor because of any other Quality whatsoever; but because they are Two. God is a Being infinite and eternal: Does it therefore follow that nothing can be distinct from him, because his Immensity includes all Space, and his Eternity exhausts all Duration? This Arguing, if it was just, (as indeed it is no Argument at all,) would lead further than this Learned Author seems to perceive.

blocks.text: Space is Eternal, but it is not therefore God. If Matter were Infinite and Eternal, still it would not at all be our God. And if any other Being had any other Attributes whatsoever, yet still if it had not Dominion over Us, Neither should We owe any Duty to It. 'Tis Dominion only, that makes God to be God to Us; and therefore the Scripture so frequently uses the word τωντοκραττωρ, Supreme over all, as equivalent to the Title, God. Now in the Notion of Dominion, 'tis very evident that original and derived are Distinctions which make a plain and necessary Difference. Which is all that I contend for.

blocks.text: ANSW. There is This Difference between the Two Manners of Expression; that the latter is very clear and intelligible, the former is very dark and ambiguous. For if by the Divine Nature be meant Divine Powers, Dominion and Dignity; then they are only Two different manners of expressling One and the Same Thing. But if by The Divine Nature be meant (as this Learned Author seems to understand it,) individually God himself; then the Father's communicating the Divine Nature to the Son, is as much as to say, his communicating HIMSELF [his individual Self] to the Son. Which, far from being an Explication of Scripture, is on the contrary infinitely harder to understand, than any thing we meet withal in Scripture.

To whom, if what I have offered has Weight and Truth on its side, it will, I make no doubt, approve itself: If it has not, I am content it should find no better Reception than it deserves. I desire not, to impose my Opinion upon any Man; but only to prevail with Men to study the Scripture, and to make It their only Rule in matters of Revelation; and that inquisitive Persons would be pleased to Compare what has been or shall be objected against me, with what I have said either in Answer to, or in order to obviate, such Objections. It would be endless for me to repeat the same things again and again, as often as any one shall please to tell the World he differs from me, without offering any New Arguments for such his Opinion. Whenever either my own further Searches, or the learned Enquiries of Others, convince me that I am mistaken in my present Notions, I shall think my self obliged to own it to the World. In the mean time I hope I may without Offense desire, that if I am Silent hereafter, it may be interpreted as a Declaration, that I see no reason to change my Sentiments. Several false Notions of the Conditions of Salvation are considered, particularly of being saved by Faith. Of trusting to external performances. Of the power of Charity to cover Sins. Of relying upon the Merits of Christ. Of Man's Weakness, and God's Grace. Of Repentance. Of the Example of the Thief upon the Cross. Of trusting to a Death-bed Sorrow. Of the Parable of the Labourers in the Vineyard. Of depending upon Amendment in Time to come. pr. 5 s.
The Reasonableness of Conformity to the Church of England. In two Parts. With the Defense of it; and the Persuasive to Lay-Conformity. The Third Edition. To which is added, The brief Defense of Episcopal Ordination. Together with the Reply to the Introduction to the Second Part; and a Postscript relating to the Third Part, of Mr. Calamy's Defense of Moderate Non-conformity. pr. 6s.
